summary:
Flame in Freefall turns a sampled collection of combustion records into an interactive research workspace. Users can inspect original evidence, compare experimental conditions, rank relevance to a habitat scenario, and export a traceable research brief.

The official challenge asks participants to make microgravity combustion findings easier to summarize, rank and interpret for space-exploration fire-safety research. A useful comparison starts with knowing what was tested, which conditions are comparable, and where the evidence stops.

Our approach puts traceability before inference. Each experimental row retains its identity, original source fields, units, missing values and quality flags. The interface separates experimental evidence from historical context, and makes ranking assumptions visible rather than hiding them behind a single score.

The intended users are students, hackathon researchers and people exploring combustion literature. The potential benefit is a shorter path from a habitat question to a source-backed comparison. Time savings and scientific outcomes have not been measured in a user study.

This release implements deterministic relevance scoring and extractive keyword retrieval. It does not run a generative model or claim super-intelligence, autonomous scientific reasoning, or validated fire-safety predictions. This is a concrete boundary relative to the challenge's broader SI ambition.
details:
What It Does & How It Works?

Flame in Freefall transforms a sampled snapshot of NASA Physical Science Informatics (PSI) records (the FLARE-X 0.3.1 dataset, containing 181 experimental rows across 12 PSI investigations and 85 historical context records) into a browser-based research tool.

• Workflow (Find → Inspect → Compare → Rank → Export): Users define a target habitat environment (such as a Lunar habitat at 30% oxygen and 10.2 psi), and the Scenario Ranker deterministically scores experimental rows based on condition similarity (60% oxygen/pressure, 25% airflow, and 15% numeric availability).

• Interactive Views: Users can visualize compatible data points on an Oxygen–Pressure Condition Map, search records in Explore, inspect row-level raw CSV cells and quality flags via evidence drawers, shortlist up to three experiments side-by-side in Compare, and search live public NASA NTRS publications in the Research Desk.

• Traceable Exports: Researchers can export Markdown or JSON briefs that preserve all original source fields, ranking assumptions, citations, and missing-data notes.

Benefits & Intended Impact

• Benefits: It eliminates the friction of manually sifting through fragmented experimental records by providing a no-login, zero-installation web workspace that surfaces exact experimental parameters alongside unresolved source conflicts.

• Intended Impact: Designed for students, hackathon participants, and space-exploration researchers, the project shortens the path from asking a habitat fire-safety question to building a source-backed evidence comparison without risking AI hallucinations.

Tools, Languages, & Architecture

• Frontend & Styling: Next.js (App Router), React, TypeScript (static export), and locally hosted Newsreader and Public Sans typography.

• Data Processing & Backend: Python 3 (for checksum validation and dataset importing), a same-origin Worker API (worker/nasa.mjs) to proxy and cache live NASA NTRS literature searches, and browser-local storage for user shortlists.

• 3D & Design Assets: Three.js (GLTFLoader) to render a custom 3D mascot guide, Meshy for 3D asset generation, and OpenAI Codex for implementation refinement and automated testing.

• Runtime Environment: Built to run on Node.js 22+ with zero external database dependencies or required API keys for end users.

Creativity

• Traceability Over Black-Box AI: Rather than using a generative model to guess fire probabilities, the project pairs a deterministic, user-adjustable relevance rubric with extractive retrieval, visualizing data gaps (such as plotting 35 compatible coordinate pairs while explicitly quarantining 146 unmapped rows).

• Tactile Editorial Aesthetic & 3D Onboarding: Moving away from generic dark-mode dashboards, the interface uses a warm paper, charcoal, and restrained orange visual system. It also features an optional, lightweight (1.42 MB) 3D EmberCosmos avatar that introduces the six workspace sections with full reduced-motion and text fallbacks.

Key Factors Considered by the Team

• Data Integrity & Epistemic Honesty: The team strictly separated experimental results (100 rows) from conditions-only setups (73 rows), excluded 8 planned test matrices from rankings, and refused to guess unknown units or fill in missing values.

• Scientific Boundaries: The interface explicitly clarifies that relevance scores measure parameter similarity—not fire probability—and that microgravity data cannot be assumed equivalent to lunar or Martian gravity.

• Performance & Accessibility: The 3D mascot was compressed from 24.44 MB down to 1.42 MB and lazy-loaded only when triggered, ensuring fast load times alongside fallback caches in case live NASA NTRS endpoints are unavailable.
